## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes the deployment and operation of static (closed,
non-flow-through) chambers for manual measurement of soil CO~2~ efflux
in the field. Static chambers are a simple, low-cost method for
quantifying soil respiration across treatments, land uses, or seasonal
gradients when the Picarro CRDS automated system
([SOP-F504](SOP-F504-picarro-field-deployment.qmd)) is not available
or when additional spatial replication is needed. The method captures
headspace gas samples at timed intervals, which are analyzed for CO~2~
concentration using a portable infrared gas analyzer (IRGA), syringe
samples returned to the lab, or soda-lime traps
[@hutchinson1981; @livingston1995; @parkin2012].

The static chamber method remains one of the most widely used
approaches for point-scale soil CO~2~ flux measurement because of its
simplicity and low cost, though it is subject to known biases from
headspace concentration buildup and pressure artifacts [@pumpanen2004;
@rochette2005]. At a global scale, soil respiration represents one of
the largest fluxes in the terrestrial carbon cycle, and small changes
can have significant implications for atmospheric CO~2~ concentrations
[@raich1992; @davidson2002].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Manual static chamber measurements of soil CO~2~
  efflux at EA Program field sites; applicable to grasslands,
  agricultural plots, restoration sites, and forest soils
- **Does not apply to:** Automated dynamic chambers with the Picarro
  CRDS analyzer (see [SOP-F504](SOP-F504-picarro-field-deployment.qmd));
  eddy covariance or gradient flux methods; aquatic CO~2~ flux
  measurements; N~2~O or CH~4~ flux measurements requiring GC or CRDS
  analysis (though the same chambers can be used with different
  analytical endpoints)
- **Location:** All EA Program terrestrial field sites


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve chamber design and deployment plan              |
| Trained Personnel | Install collars, deploy chambers, collect gas samples   |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use                |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Driving collars into soil with a mallet poses impact
  injury risk. Carrying chambers and equipment over uneven terrain.
- **Heat:** Southern California field sites can exceed 40 C. Metal
  chambers become extremely hot in direct sunlight; handle with gloves.
- **Chemical:** Soda-lime (NaOH/Ca(OH)~2~) is corrosive and causes
  burns on skin and eye contact. Concentrated NaOH solutions used for
  soda-lime traps are hazardous. Handle with gloves and safety glasses.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Nitrile or leather gloves
- [ ] Safety glasses (when handling soda-lime or driving collars)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)

### Related SOPs

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd) for general
field safety procedures.


## 5. Equipment and Materials

| Item                          | Notes                                     |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| PVC or metal collars          | Installed in the soil at least 24 hours before measurement |
| Chamber lids                  | Opaque (dark) for total respiration; clear for net CO~2~ exchange |
| Rubber mallet                 | For installing collars                    |
| Sealing material              | Closed-cell foam gasket or water trough on collar rim |
| Syringes (30--60 mL)          | For headspace gas sampling (syringe method) |
| Evacuated vials (Exetainer)   | For storing gas samples for lab analysis  |
| Portable IRGA (optional)      | For real-time CO~2~ concentration readings |
| Soda-lime (optional)          | For absorption-based CO~2~ measurement    |
| Timer or stopwatch            | For tracking deployment intervals          |
| Thermometer or soil temp probe | For concurrent soil temperature            |
| Soil moisture probe (optional) | TDR or capacitance sensor                 |
| Ruler or tape measure         | For measuring headspace height             |
| Field data sheet              | For recording deployment times and readings |
| GPS unit or smartphone        | For recording chamber locations             |


## 6. Procedure

### 6.1 Collar Installation

1. Install PVC or metal collars into the soil to a depth of
   approximately 5 cm at least 24 hours (preferably 48 hours) before
   the first measurement to allow the soil to recover from
   disturbance.
2. Do not sever major roots during installation; if roots are
   encountered, reposition slightly.
3. Measure and record the collar inside diameter and the height of the
   collar above the soil surface on at least two sides. These
   dimensions are needed to calculate headspace volume.

### 6.2 Chamber Deployment

1. Record the start time, soil temperature (at 5 cm depth), and soil
   moisture at each collar location.
2. Place the chamber lid on the collar, ensuring a gas-tight seal
   (foam gasket compressed or water trough filled).
3. If using the syringe method, collect a headspace sample immediately
   after sealing (time zero), then at regular intervals (e.g., 10, 20,
   30, and 40 minutes). The choice of deployment interval (typically
   20--45 minutes) represents a trade-off: shorter deployments reduce
   the concentration-feedback bias that suppresses diffusion as
   headspace CO~2~ rises, but longer deployments provide a more
   detectable concentration change in low-flux soils [@hutchinson1981;
   @pumpanen2004].
4. If using a portable IRGA, connect the chamber to the analyzer and
   record CO~2~ concentration continuously or at 1-minute intervals.
5. If using soda-lime traps, weigh the pre-dried soda-lime, place it
   inside the sealed chamber, and retrieve it after a fixed deployment
   period (typically 24 hours). Re-dry and reweigh to determine CO~2~
   absorbed.

### 6.3 Ending the Measurement

1. Remove the chamber lid at the end of the measurement period.
2. Record the end time.
3. Transfer syringe samples to evacuated vials (Exetainers) for
   transport to the lab if not using IRGA.


## 7. Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

### 7.1 Flux Calculation

**Linear method (syringe or IRGA):**

$$
F = \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta t} \times \frac{V}{A} \times \frac{P}{RT}
$$

where $F$ = CO~2~ flux (micromol m^-2^ s^-1^), $\Delta C / \Delta t$ =
rate of change in headspace CO~2~ concentration (ppm s^-1^), $V$ =
headspace volume (m^3^), $A$ = collar area (m^2^), $P$ = atmospheric
pressure (Pa), $R$ = ideal gas constant (8.314 J mol^-1^ K^-1^), and
$T$ = air temperature (K).

**Soda-lime method:**

$$
F = \frac{(M_f - M_i) \times 1.69}{A \times t}
$$

where $M_f$ and $M_i$ are the final and initial soda-lime masses (g),
1.69 is the stoichiometric correction factor, $A$ = collar area (m^2^),
and $t$ = deployment time (hours).

### 7.2 QC Requirements

- Deploy at least three replicate chambers per treatment or land use.
- Inspect collar seals before each deployment. Soil settling or animal
  disturbance can break the seal.
- Record soil temperature and moisture alongside every flux
  measurement; these are the primary drivers of soil respiration. Soil
  respiration typically increases exponentially with temperature, with
  Q~10~ values of 2--3 [@raich1992; @bond-lamberty2010]. Reporting
  concurrent soil temperature and moisture allows flux values to be
  normalized or modeled across campaigns and sites.
- Reject any measurement where the R^2^ of the linear regression
  (concentration vs. time) is below 0.90, unless the flux is near
  zero.
- Avoid measuring during or immediately after rainfall, as water
  pooling on the collar disrupts gas exchange.


## 8. Waste Disposal

| Waste Type              | Disposal Method                             |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Used soda-lime          | Allow to dry; dispose as solid waste (non-hazardous once fully carbonated) |
| Syringe needles         | Sharps container                            |
| Used gloves             | Standard trash                              |

## 11. Training Record

Before deploying soil respiration chambers independently, personnel
must:

1. Read this SOP and [SOP-F504](SOP-F504-picarro-field-deployment.qmd)
   in full
2. Demonstrate proper collar installation and headspace volume
   measurement
3. Perform a supervised syringe sampling or IRGA measurement at one
   site
4. Calculate flux from field data and demonstrate agreement with the
   trainer's calculation
5. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
